analysis.one_liner: Bans racial profiling by all law enforcement and ties federal police grants to anti-profiling policies.
analysis.headline: The End Racial Profiling Act of 2011, backed by 18 Senate Democrats, never received a committee vote or a floor vote, dying after one subcommittee hearing in April 2012.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it illegal for any federal, state, local, or tribal law enforcement agent to rely on race, ethnicity, national origin, or religion when deciding whom to stop, search, or investigate, except when there is specific information linking a person of that background to an actual crime. It would have let people hurt by profiling sue in court to stop it, required federal agencies to adopt anti-profiling policies, required states to certify they had done the same before receiving Justice Department grant money, and created nationwide data collection on who gets stopped and searched. It never made it out of the Senate Judiciary Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers, pedestrians, and travelers who get stopped or searched, especially Black, Latino, Muslim, Sikh, and other minority communities where profiling is documented. The bill would also have given individuals the right to sue for a court order stopping profiling practices, with attorney's fees available to people who win.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People profiled in stops and searches

how_it_helps.text: No law enforcement agent or agency — federal, state, local, or tribal — could rely on race, ethnicity, national origin, or religion in routine stops, searches, interviews, or immigration and customs investigations, unless trustworthy information linked a person of that background to an identified crime.

An individual injured by racial profiling, or the United States, could sue for a court order to stop the practice, and proof that a jurisdiction's stops and searches have a disparate impact on racial, ethnic, or religious minorities would count as initial evidence of a violation. Winning plaintiffs could recover attorney's fees.

States, local governments, and tribal agencies would have to certify they maintain anti-profiling policies, training, and data collection before receiving money from the Byrne Justice Assistance Grant and Cops on the Beat programs, and the Attorney General could withhold grants from noncompliant recipients.

Law enforcement agencies would have to collect standardized data on who gets stopped and searched — by race, ethnicity, national origin, gender, and religion — and the Justice Department would publish annual public reports analyzing disparities in stops and in 'hit rates' (how often searches actually find contraband).

analysis.who_pays: Law enforcement agencies, which would bear the cost of new training, data collection systems, complaint procedures, and audits. Police departments that did not comply could lose federal grant money, and departments with disparate stop patterns could face civil lawsuits.

drawbacks.text: The bill covers immigration and customs enforcement as well as police, and bars reliance on religion or national origin in workplace immigration investigations and border interviews more extensive than customary checks — critics argue this ties the hands of agents enforcing immigration and counterterrorism law.

The compliance burden is real: departments would need new data collection technology, standardized reporting to the Justice Department, complaint procedures or independent audits, and training, with small and rural agencies given a share of grant money specifically to help absorb the cost.
Because a disparate impact on minorities would count as initial evidence of a violation, departments with skewed stop statistics could face litigation even where officers claim neutral motives.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people who are stopped or searched based on their race, ethnicity, or religion, the bill offered a direct remedy: a legal prohibition, a private right to sue, and federal grant money conditioned on compliance. The costs fall on law enforcement agencies, which would have to document their stops and change training — costs the bill itself partially offsets with best-practices and technology grants. The disparate-impact litigation standard is the strongest good-faith objection, but the bill's own data provision exists precisely to distinguish real profiling from neutral policing, since equal 'hit rates' across groups would show stops are not race-based.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, got a single subcommittee hearing in April 2012, and was never reported to the full Senate or voted on before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Benjamin Cardin introduced the bill on October 6, 2011, joined by 17 Democratic cosponsors and no Republicans, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day.

The Judiciary Committee's Subcommittee on Constitution, Civil Rights and Human Rights held a hearing on the bill on April 17, 2012, but the full committee never took it up and the Senate never voted on it.
The bill sat in committee until the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, and no version of it became law in that Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Law enforcement agencies are better off because the bill died: they avoided mandatory anti-profiling policies, public stop-and-search data collection, grant conditions, and the prospect of disparate-impact lawsuits. People subject to profiling gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Law enforcement agencies avoiding new oversight

for.name: Sen. Benjamin Cardin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor on October 6 and October 13, 2011.

for.name: 17 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; the bill's entire support in the Senate was Democratic.

for.name: Judiciary Subcommittee on Constitution, Civil Rights and Human Rights
for.role: Subcommittee of the Senate Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Held the bill's only hearing, on April 17, 2012, with a printed hearing record.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Full committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or reported the bill to the full Senate after referring it on October 6, 2011, so no vote ever occurred.

sides.party_line_note: All 18 sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored it; because the bill never reached a vote, there is no roll call showing where the parties stood beyond sponsorship.

industries.industry: Law enforcement agencies (federal, state, local, and tribal police and immigration/customs enforcement)
industries.note: The bill would have imposed mandatory anti-profiling policies, training, standardized data collection, complaint procedures, and exposure to disparate-impact lawsuits, and could have cut off Byrne and COPS grant money to departments that did not comply. Departments that stop and search minority residents at higher rates would have had those patterns published in annual Justice Department reports.

industries.industry: Grant-funded policing programs (Byrne Justice Assistance Grants, Cops on the Beat)
industries.note: The bill conditions this funding on anti-profiling compliance but also authorizes new grants for training, data technology, and audit systems, with a reserved share for small and rural agencies. Departments that already follow fair policing practices lose nothing.
